results.summary: This analog block reimplements the behaviour of a 555 timer, with threshold, trigger, discharge, reset and output pins exposed for external RC networks. It is intended to be wired on a breadboard with through-hole resistors and capacitors and configured in astable or monostable circuits taken from a 555 datasheet. A tester built the suggested astable circuit with 4.7k resistors and roughly 15uF capacitance and observed about 10Hz on the output. The design is notable for being a transistor-level analog clone of a classic part rather than a digital timer, and its maximum frequency was not established.

This analog tile collects separate PLL building blocks: two phase frequency detectors, a charge pump, a ring-oscillator VCO and four D flip-flop frequency dividers, each contributed by a different participant of the Saudi Semiconductor Program. Testing requires a two-channel function generator to drive the PFD and divider inputs and a two-channel oscilloscope to observe the QA/QB pulses, charge-pump output and divided frequencies. The VCO is tuned by a control voltage around 0.75V to 1V, and the dividers are expected to produce one-eighth of a 40 to 80MHz input. The blocks are documented individually but are not wired together into a complete closed-loop PLL on this tile.

This Verilog design implements modified-consensus voting for redundant microcontrollers, treating each of the eight inputs as a vote where 1 means fail and 0 means pass. The number of active voters and the failure threshold are configurable, so a system can, for example, fail when three of eight voters report a fault. It is aimed at safety-critical hardware where redundant controllers guard against single-point faults. Verification is done through unit tests run with make in the test subfolder, and no external hardware is described.

This project is a 4-bit Wallace tree multiplier written in Verilog, built from instantiated half-adder and full-adder modules. It takes two 4-bit operands on the eight input pins and presents the product on the eight outputs. A testbench named wallace_tb.v is provided to exercise the design. The documentation is brief and does not report synthesis results or silicon measurements.

This Wokwi project is a 3-bit asynchronous down counter in which each flip-flop clocks the next, with a button used to advance the count. It is meant to drive a 7-segment display as external hardware. A tester ran it through the Commander application and found that ui_in[0] acts as the clock rather than the real clock, and that the observed output sequence 102, 63, 7, 79, 109, 6, 125, 91 repeats, suggesting the output bits are scrambled relative to the intended display. The silicon behaviour therefore only partially matches the intended counter.

This Wokwi design is a digital dice that displays the word roll and lights the number 6 as a lucky result. The user interacts with it through a switch, and the documentation gives no further detail on the internal logic or how the value is generated. No external hardware beyond the on-board display and switch is mentioned. The description is very thin, so the exact behaviour and any randomness cannot be confirmed from the provided text.

This Wokwi project lets a user select a number from 1 to 8 with DIP switches and indicates whether it is even or odd using LEDs and a 7-segment display, with logic gates such as AND, OR, XOR, NAND and NOT involved. Switching on 2, 4, 6 or 8 is intended to light all blue LEDs and show 8 on the display. A tester confirmed that the odd/even detection works on silicon but that the 7-segment output does not match the Wokwi simulation because the display is wired differently on the board. The project is a logic-gate teaching exercise and needs an external seven-segment display.

This Wokwi puzzle uses eight DIP switches, each mapped to a Notre Dame dormitory, and lights an LED when a valid combination of three dorms is selected. The valid set requires one of the best male dorms, one of the best female dorms and the best gender-neutral dorm, for example Alumni, Flaherty and Fischer Grad. It is intended as a trial-and-error exercise for students learning about logic gates. One external LED is needed, and no silicon test results are reported.

This Wokwi design drives a 7-segment display to spell out PILIPINASLASALLE one character per clock cycle, with the decimal point toggling each cycle. Setting input pin 7 high enables a manual mode in which pins 0 to 3 select a BCD value that maps to a specific character according to a documented table. It is based on an earlier Wokwi project and requires an external 7-segment display. Multiple testers, including the author, report that the message appears correctly on silicon and that manual mode works, although one tester noted the reset signal appears to have no effect and the sequence starts at a random point.

This Wokwi project is described only as a microchip that lights an LED digital number and an LED, controlled by flicking switches in the simulation. No pin functions, logic details or external hardware requirements are documented. Testing is limited to starting the Wokwi simulation and toggling switches. The documentation is essentially a placeholder, so the design's actual behaviour cannot be determined.
